title: A Lightweight Lung Segmentation and Vision Transformer Framework for CT-Based Lung Cancer Classification.
abstract: Lung cancer remains a major cause of cancer-related mortality, and accurate analysis of pulmonary abnormalities on computed tomography (CT) images is important for supporting timely diagnosis. However, automated lung cancer classification remains challenging because pulmonary lesions exhibit substantial variability in size, morphology, intensity, and anatomical location, while image noise and irrelevant surrounding structures can adversely affect model performance. This study investigates an integrated deep learning framework combining image restoration, anatomical segmentation, and transformer-based classification for computer-aided lung cancer analysis. The proposed framework consists of three sequential stages. First, Fast Non-Local Means (FNLM) denoising is applied to reduce image noise while preserving relevant anatomical structures. Second, lung regions are isolated using intensity-based thresholding followed by morphological operations and contour-based refinement. The resulting lung masks are applied to the denoised CT images to suppress irrelevant surrounding structures. Finally, the segmented lung images are resized and normalized and supplied to a Vision Transformer (ViT), which learns contextual representations for classification. The framework is evaluated using a single open-access CT image dataset under two classification settings: binary classification of cancerous and non-cancerous CT images and multiclass discrimination among normal, benign, and malignant cases. In binary lung cancer classification, the proposed framework correctly classified 982 of 1000 CT images, achieving an accuracy of 98.20%, with sensitivity, specificity, precision, and F1 scores of 98.20%. For multiclass classification of normal, benign, and malignant cases, the framework correctly classified 951 of 1005 CT images, corresponding to an overall accuracy of 94.63%. Class-wise precision, recall, specificity, F1 score, and ROC-AUC were additionally evaluated to provide a more comprehensive assessment of classification performance. These findings reflect performance under the evaluated experimental conditions. The proposed framework demonstrates promising performance for CT-based lung cancer classification by integrating FNLM denoising, conventional lung-region extraction, and transformer-based representation learning. However, because the evaluation relied on a single open-access dataset with image-level partitioning, the generalizability of the findings to independent patient populations and clinical settings remains uncertain. Further patient-disjoint evaluation, external validation using multi-institutional datasets, and prospective clinical assessment are required before its potential clinical utility can be established.

title: Multiparametric MRI Radiomics and MAID-CDF Texture Descriptors for Preoperative Three-Class Histopathological Grading of Endometrial Carcinoma.
abstract: Background/Objectives: To evaluate a multiparametric MRI machine-learning framework for preoperative three-class histopathological grading of endometrial carcinoma using conventional radiomics, Multiradius Annular Intensity-Difference cumulative-distribution-function descriptors (MAID-CDF), stability-based feature selection, and decision-level multimodal fusion. Methods: This retrospective single-center study included 96 patients (Grade 1, n=26; Grade 2, n=40; Grade 3, n=30). Quantitative features were derived from contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI (T1+C), T2-weighted MRI, and ADC maps. Model development used stratified five-fold outer cross-validation, with Elastic-Net stability selection and hyperparameter optimization performed within each training partition before support vector machine classification. Multimodal predictions were combined by hard voting, soft voting, and cross-fitted Random-Forest stacking. Performance was calculated from pooled out-of-fold predictions. The primary models were also assessed using ten independently seeded repetitions of stratified five-fold nested cross-validation. Results: T1+C, T2, and ADC models achieved accuracies of 88.5%, 89.6%, and 92.7% and macro-F1 scores of 0.884, 0.891, and 0.925, respectively. ADC had the highest single-modality macro-AUC (0.971). Hard and soft voting each achieved 93.8% accuracy and a macro-F1 of 0.937; soft voting yielded a macro-AUC of 0.989. The Random-Forest stack achieved 90.6% accuracy, a macro-F1 of 0.904, and a macro-AUC of 0.985. For ADC, adding MAID-CDF to radiomics increased Grade 3 sensitivity from 80.0% to 93.3%, although a paired exact test did not establish a significant difference for Grade 3 sensitivity. Across ten repetitions, soft voting achieved 93.0% ± 1.1% accuracy and macro-F1 of 0.929 ± 0.012; the combined ADC model achieved 90.2% ± 2.2% accuracy and macro-F1 of 0.897 ± 0.022. Conclusions: The framework achieved high internally validated performance for three-class grading. ADC provided the strongest single-modality results, while the contribution of MAID-CDF was modality dependent and appeared most favorable with ADC radiomics. These findings support further evaluation of complementary quantitative MRI representations for preoperative grading. Repeated partitioning supported the relative consistency of soft voting, whereas the additional contribution of MAID-CDF varied across performance measures.

title: Is the Donor Part of the Product? A Systematic Review of Patient Factors Affecting Platelet-Rich Plasma and Bone Marrow Aspirate Concentrate Composition and Clinical Response.
abstract: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) and bone marrow aspirate concentrate (BMAC) vary in composition and are associated with heterogeneous clinical outcomes. We examined donor, procedural, and disease-related factors associated with product composition and clinical prognosis. Six databases and registers were searched. Eighteen human studies were included. Two independent reviewers assessed risk of bias using Quality in Prognosis Studies (QUIPS), and certainty was rated using a Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE)-informed approach. Because of heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively. Thirteen studies concerned PRP (seven composition, six clinical) and five concerned BMAC (three composition, two clinical). Baseline whole-blood platelet count was positively associated with final PRP platelet concentration in two studies (low-certainty evidence), without establishing greater administered platelet dose or clinical benefit. BMAC cellular yield varied with harvesting conditions and cellular assay definitions; demographic associations were inconsistent. Associations between radiographic osteoarthritis severity and outcomes after PRP were heterogeneous and of very-low certainty. Donor biology and processing characteristics are associated with selected orthobiologic product measures, but corresponding clinical implications remain uncertain. Single-arm prognostic studies cannot establish treatment-effect modification or composition-mediated benefit. PROSPERO CRD420261483107. Level III; systematic review of predominantly observational and prognostic-factor studies.

title: Artificial Intelligence for the Molecular Diagnosis of Kidney Diseases: From Computational Pathology to Noninvasive Multi-Omics.
abstract: Creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate and histology detect kidney disease late and say little about the molecular heterogeneity driving progression. Artificial intelligence can extract molecular features from biofluid omics; digitised biopsies and retinal images supply proxy readouts, not molecular measurements. In this review we grouped the literature by histopathology, multi-omics, foundation models and noninvasive systems and checked each result against its cohort, endpoint and validation setting. Reported performance is often high, but most results come from retrospective single-cohort evaluations; external and prospective validation are uncommon, and we found no study among those reviewed showing improved patient outcomes. High discrimination therefore establishes technical performance only; clinical utility and patient benefit remain untested. The evidence to date supports feasibility, not benefit, and the weakness lies in evaluation design rather than model architecture. The evidence so far establishes feasibility, not benefit. Until prospective studies on shared external cohorts are available, these tools are best used to augment existing diagnostic practice, with patient outcomes as the measure of success.

title: A Dual-Encoder Feature Fusion Framework for Pseudo-Healthy Reconstruction in 3D Brain MRI Anomaly Detection.
abstract: Detecting diverse lesions in brain MRI is clinically important. Unsupervised anomaly detection methods have attracted widespread attention because they learn healthy patterns to detect anomalies without lesion annotations. Among them, reconstruction-based methods generate a pseudo-healthy image (PHI) and localize lesions using reconstruction errors. However, existing methods struggle to suppress anomaly reconstruction while recovering normal details. To address this challenge, we propose a pseudo-healthy image reconstruction framework based on dual-encoder feature fusion. A structural reference encoder takes binary edge maps as input to extract structural features and limit the direct propagation of abnormal intensity information. An appearance detail encoder extracts appearance features from the original image to supplement normal tissue details. Discrepancy-guided adaptive fusion uses structural reference features as an anchor to regulate appearance contributions according to local feature discrepancies. At local positions with larger discrepancies, appearance weights are reduced to limit the introduction of abnormal information; at positions with smaller discrepancies, more appearance details are incorporated to improve normal tissue reconstruction. A shared decoder reconstructs a PHI from the fused features. Across eight brain MRI datasets (3055 volumes), our method outperforms 16 baselines, improving average precision and Dice similarity coefficient by 4.15 and 3.19 percentage points over the strongest baseline.

title: DeepSkin: A Segmentation-Guided Deep Learning Framework with Generative Augmentation for Dermoscopic Skin Cancer Classification.
abstract: Artificial intelligence has considerable potential to support dermoscopic skin cancer assessment; however, class imbalance, heterogeneous lesion morphology, indistinct lesion boundaries, and imaging variability can limit model generalizability. This study presents DeepSkin, a segmentation-guided deep learning framework integrating lesion segmentation, generative augmentation, and lesion-focused classification. Dermoscopic images were first segmented using a bidirectional ConvLSTM-based U-Net (BCDU-Net), and the resulting lesion regions were used for region-of-interest (ROI) extraction. During classifier development, a conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) generated class-conditioned synthetic lesion ROIs to increase training-data diversity and mitigate class imbalance. Real and synthetic training ROIs were subsequently used to train a fine-tuned VGG16 network for binary benign-malignant classification. The framework was developed using the ISIC 2016 dataset, comprising 900 training and 379 test images, and independently evaluated on the PH2 dataset. On ISIC 2016, DeepSkin achieved a Dice coefficient of 0.937 and an intersection over union (IoU) of 0.882 for lesion segmentation, together with a classification accuracy of 96.6% and a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.981. Cross-dataset external evaluation on the independent PH2 dataset, conducted without retraining or fine-tuning, yielded a classification accuracy of 95%. Ablation analysis further demonstrated incremental performance improvements associated with preprocessing, segmentation-guided ROI extraction, and generative augmentation. Grad-CAM visualizations provided qualitative insight into image regions contributing to classification decisions. These findings suggest that integrating generative augmentation with segmentation-guided lesion classification can support accurate dermoscopic image analysis across independent datasets. Further evaluation using larger, diverse, multi-center and prospective clinical datasets is required to establish broader generalizability and clinical applicability.

title: Clinically Informed Optic Disc and Optic Cup Segmentation for Automated Glaucoma Assessment Using Adaptive Feature Fusion Multi-Task U-Net+.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Glaucoma is considered one of the most serious eye diseases leading to permanent vision loss worldwide. Early diagnosis and regular follow-up are crucial for slowing disease progression and preserving visual function. Accurate segmentation of the optic disc (OD) and optic cup (OC) from fundus images enables reliable estimation of clinically important biomarkers such as the cup-to-disc ratio (CDR). However, the low contrast of OC boundaries, vascular occlusions, and variations in image acquisition conditions continue to limit the performance of automated segmentation methods. This study proposes a novel deep learning framework, Adaptive Feature Fusion Multi-Task U-Net++ (AFF-MT U-Net++), for accurate OD and OC segmentation. Methods: The proposed architecture incorporates an EfficientNet-B5-based encoder, an Adaptive Feature Fusion (AFF) module for refining feature representations, a boundary-aware learning strategy for improving anatomical boundary localization, and a clinical feature learning branch that models structural indicators related to glaucoma assessment. The proposed method was evaluated on 1200 eligible annotated images retained from the REFUGE2 dataset after data screening using a source-stratified, image-level five-fold cross-validation protocol on the pooled REFUGE2 data and compared with U-Net, U-Net++, nnU-Net, and PVTv2 models. Results: Experimental results demonstrated that the proposed method achieved a Dice score of 0.8910 ± 0.0023 and an Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.8035 ± 0.0037 for OC segmentation, while obtaining a Dice score of 0.9602 ± 0.0016 and an IoU of 0.9235 ± 0.0029 for OD segmentation. In addition, the model achieved a vertical cup-to-disc ratio error (δvCDR) of 0.0433 ± 0.0011. Paired statistical comparisons indicated higher Dice and IoU scores and lower δvCDR errors than the evaluated baseline models, although improvements were not observed for every metric. Conclusions: AFF-MT U-Net++ provided reliable and stable OD/OC segmentation performance on the REFUGE2 dataset through adaptive multi-scale feature fusion, boundary-aware learning, and clinical feature modeling. The proposed framework produced anatomically consistent segmentation results and demonstrated its potential to support computer-aided glaucoma assessment from fundus images.

title: Temporal Prior-Guided Segmentation of Pulmonary Lesions in Longitudinal CT: Input-Level Versus Prompt-Level Prior Injection.
abstract: Background/Objectives: In longitudinal computed tomography follow-up, lesion boundaries from the previous timepoint are routinely available but usually encoded as binary masks for automated segmentation. We convert the expert-drawn t - 1 reference mask into a continuous spatial prior through exponential distance encoding, without providing the previous image to the network, and examine whether the site at which this prior is injected matters more than its resolution or encoding. Methods: A total of 244 sequential t - 1 → t pairs from 136 patients at a single centre were analysed with patient-level five-fold cross-validation. The prior was injected into a network built on Segment Anything Model 2 either as a full-resolution fourth input channel or on the stride-16 grid via the pretrained mask-prompt encoder; a control arm reduced the channel prior to the same 32 × 32 grid, and a further arm was trained with the prior binarised. The four-channel and prior-free arms were replicated with EVA-02. Comparators were a copy-forward baseline and a two-channel nnU-Net. Results: The four-channel model reached a mean Dice of 0.739, significantly exceeding the prior-free model at 0.672, while copy-forward reached 0.410. In 27 pairs with no mask-target overlap, it still achieved 0.575, compared with 0.482 without the prior (p = 0.08). The prompt pathway reached 0.715, whereas the 32 × 32 control retained the full gain (0.743 vs. 0.739; 95% confidence interval [CI] of the difference -0.013 to +0.021) and exceeded the prompt pathway even in lesions spanning 1-2 stride-16 cells. An arm trained with a binary prior matched the soft prior, indicating that the prior acts as a coarse regional cue rather than a shape template. With last-epoch weights, as used for nnU-Net, the four-channel model matched nnU-Net in mean Dice at 0.704 but had fewer complete failures and no empty predictions, compared with 14. Weighted κ for categorical change classification did not improve significantly, at 0.555 versus 0.505. Conclusions: As a soft spatial prior, the routinely available previous mask improves segmentation accuracy and markedly reduces complete misses. Where the prior enters the network matters more than its spatial resolution or its soft encoding. Without gains in categorical change detection, the method currently suits automated pre-delineation and cohort-level analysis.

title: Do Global Vessel Descriptors Help Multi-Disease Fundus Classification? A Leakage-Controlled Ablation of Hybrid CNN-Transformer Models with External Testing.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Retinal vessel features are often added to fundus classifiers without isolating their effect. We examined whether global vessel descriptors improve multi-disease fundus classification under leakage-controlled external testing. Methods: After a duplicate audit and field-of-view normalization, models were trained on RFMiD and APTOS with a partial-label mask and tested internally and on four external datasets (ODIR-5K, Mendeley, STARE, IDRiD) that were not used for training, threshold fitting or calibration. Fourteen arms were compared: nine architectures combining EfficientNet-B4, Swin-S and a vessel branch, a label-handling control, and four variants with vessel features from other segmenters; ten arms were trained with three seeds. Vessel descriptors came from segmenters trained on 14 DRIVE images, 14 FIVES images or 480 FIVES images. Paired differences were tested with a hierarchical bootstrap and Holm correction; all external comparisons are exploratory. Results: The CNN-Transformer hybrid reached an internal macro-AUROC of 0.945 ± 0.002 and a mean external macro-AUROC of 0.830 ± 0.005, exceeding the CNN baseline internally, on ODIR-5K and on Mendeley (Holm-adjusted p ≤ 0.0045) but not on STARE or IDRiD; an average of separately trained CNN and Transformer models performed similarly (0.831). Treating unassessed labels as negatives lowered ODIR-5K and Mendeley AUROC (-0.018 and -0.032). For the CNN vessel arm, FIVES test Dice of 0.662, 0.779 and 0.833 for the three segmenters was accompanied by mean external AUROC of 0.786, 0.792 and 0.805, with the clearest differences on STARE and Mendeley; no vessel arm exceeded its counterpart without vessels. Conclusions: Global vessel descriptors added no measurable value to the image backbones studied, and their effect was associated with the upstream segmentation pipeline, whose quality should therefore be reported.

title: Machine Learning and Delta Habitat Radiomics Predict Neoadjuvant Chemoradiotherapy Response in Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer: A Multicenter Study.
abstract: Background: Accurate and non-invasive prediction of response to neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (NCRT) and long-term outcomes in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC) remains challenging. This multicenter study developed and validated machine-learning (ML) classifiers based on delta habitat magnetic-resonance image (MRI) radiomics to address this unmet need. Materials and Methods: A total of 1228 LARC patients who completed NCRT across five tertiary centers were retrospectively divided into four independent datasets. Serial T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted images (DWI) acquired before and after NCRT were co-registered, and delta habitat radiomic features were extracted. Fourteen ML algorithms were trained and externally validated for three signature sets: T2 delta habitat, DWI delta habitat, and combined delta habitat. Model performance was assessed with ROC analysis, Kaplan-Meier survival curves, and decision-curve analysis (DCA). Results: Among the 14 classifier configurations evaluated, the combined T2WI+DWI delta habitat multilayer perceptron (MLP) model achieved AUCs of 0.932, 0.903, 0.925, and 0.922 in the training, validation, Test1, and Test2 cohorts, respectively. The corresponding AUCs for the T2 delta habitat model were 0.801, 0.813, 0.867, and 0.788, whereas those for the DWI delta habitat model were 0.831, 0.769, 0.895, and 0.832 for predicting NCRT response. The combined delta habitat signature provided risk stratification for disease-free and overall survival. Importantly, the combined delta habitat model also discriminated postoperative pathological categories (ypT1N0M0 and ypCR) in an exploratory analysis. Conclusions: Delta habitat MRI radiomics showed potential for predicting NCRT response in patients with LARC. Associations with survival and discrimination of postoperative pathological categories were exploratory and require further validation. The MLP-based combined delta habitat model shows promise for clinical translation.

title: Persistent Primary Hyperparathyroidism After Parathyroidectomy: Mechanisms of Failure, Precision Re-Localization, and Reoperative Management.
abstract: Persistent primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT), defined as hypercalcemia that fails to resolve or recurs within six months of parathyroidectomy, affects approximately 2-5% of operated patients and is the leading indication for parathyroid reoperation. It results mainly from missed ectopic or overlooked eutopic adenomas and unrecognized multiglandular disease and, less often, from hereditary syndromes, lithium exposure, parathyromatosis, or carcinoma. Because reoperation in a scarred neck carries higher risks of recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and permanent hypoparathyroidism, management requires rigorous biochemical confirmation, exclusion of familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia and eucalcemic parathyroid hormone (PTH) elevation, consideration of germline genetic testing, and precise re-localization. Molecular imaging has transformed re-localization: [18F]fluorocholine PET/CT achieves per-patient sensitivities above 90% in meta-analyses that mainly included patients before initial surgery, localizes disease in approximately nine in ten patients with previous neck surgery, outperforms [99mTc]Tc-sestamibi SPECT/CT and four-dimensional CT in patients with negative or inconclusive conventional imaging, and is cost-effective. PET/MRI, PET/4D-CT fusion, and selective venous sampling address the remaining gaps, whereas novel tracers such as [68Ga]Ga-trivehexin, radiomics, and artificial intelligence remain investigational. Guided by accurate localization and intraoperative PTH monitoring in experienced centers, reoperation cures approximately nine in ten patients; an exploratory pooled analysis of 1673 patients yielded a cure rate of 92.3% (95% confidence interval 89.4-94.4%), although definitions of cure and follow-up varied between series. The surgical approach should be tailored to the location of the target gland, with transcervical thymectomy or minimally invasive thoracic techniques for mediastinal glands. Calcimimetics and antiresorptive agents are alternatives for patients unfit for surgery, image-guided ablation should be reserved for carefully selected patients because long-term data after previous neck surgery are limited, and lifelong surveillance is warranted because recurrence may occur many years later. This review integrates anatomical, molecular, imaging, surgical, and medical evidence, grades the resulting recommendations, distinguishes guideline-endorsed practice from emerging approaches, and proposes an individualized, imaging-centered algorithm.

title: Report-Defined FDG-PET/CT Positivity Is Common Across the Clinical Spectrum of Well-Differentiated Pulmonary Neuroendocrine Tumors.
abstract: Background/Objectives: The clinical significance of 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake in well-differentiated pulmonary neuroendocrine tumors (WD-PulNETs) remains uncertain. We assessed the prevalence of FDG positivity in routine clinical practice. Methods: This multicenter retrospective cohort included histologically confirmed typical or atypical pulmonary carcinoids. FDG PET/CT was classified as positive or negative according to the original nuclear-medicine report. Results: Of 91 WD-PulNETs patients, 81 had sufficient data for analysis. The cohort included 67 patients (82.7%) with typical carcinoids and 14 (17.3%) with atypical carcinoids. FDG PET/CT was performed in 50 patients (61.7%), of whom 46 (92.0%; 95% CI, 81.2-96.8%) had report-defined FDG positivity in the primary pulmonary tumor. FDG positivity was observed in 39 of 42 patients (92.9%) with typical carcinoids and 7 of 8 (87.5%) with atypical carcinoids. Comparisons between patients who underwent FDG PET/CT and those who did not revealed no statistically significant differences in most evaluated clinicopathological characteristics. However, somatostatin analogue treatment was more frequent among patients who underwent FDG PET/CT (35.6% vs. 7.7%; p = 0.011). Conclusion: Report-defined FDG positivity was highly prevalent across the spectrum of WD-PulNETs, including typical carcinoids. Potential selection bias and the small number of patients preclude firm conclusions about its discriminatory or prognostic significance.

title: Biologically Inspired Selective Attention for Prostate MRI: A Segmentation-Guided Vision Transformer Framework for Computer-Aided Diagnosis.
abstract: Prostate cancer is the second most commonly diagnosed malignancy in men, yet interpretation of multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) suffers from substantial inter-observer variability and depends on scarce expert radiologists. Expert readers follow a hierarchical, coarse-to-fine visual strategy: they first localize the prostate gland and then direct focused attention to tissue within it. Inspired by this biological selective-attention mechanism, we propose a segmentation-guided framework in which a modality-aware 3D Vision Transformer (ViT) first delineates the prostate gland from T2-weighted, ADC, and DWI volumes, and the resulting anatomical mask then constrains downstream cancer detection. Global self-attention models long-range anatomical context, analogous to the integration of peripheral and foveal information in human vision. Detection was evaluated through two pathways: gray-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) texture features with classical classifiers, and a ViT classifier. On 200 patients from the public PROSTATEx cohort, the proposed segmentation model achieved a Dice Similarity Coefficient of [0.903 ± 0.033] versus [0.898 ± 0.034] for an optimized U-Net. Ablation experiments confirmed that anatomical guidance improved both pathways. These results show that emulating expert visual search strategies yields accurate and interpretable computer-aided prostate cancer diagnosis.

title: Radiomics-Based Prediction of Bone Metastases from Baseline Prostate MRI in Prostate Cancer: A Systematic Review and Critical Appraisal.
abstract: Introduction Whether bone metastasis is present at diagnosis determines curative versus systemic treatment of prostate cancer, yet referral for advanced staging relies on imperfect risk stratification; magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) radiomics has been proposed to predict metastatic status from routinely acquired staging imaging. Methods This systematic review (PROSPERO CRD420261463568) searched PubMed, Embase and Cochrane CENTRAL for studies of radiomic, deep-learning or hybrid models predicting bone-metastatic status from prostate MRI; incremental value over clinical predictors, reporting completeness, radiomics methodology and risk of bias were appraised. Results Six retrospective studies (1240 patients, 491 with bone metastasis, all from China; 322 contributed to the principal validation estimates) were included. Clinical-plus-radiomics models achieved validation areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) of 0.893-0.920 internally and 0.903 externally, with the highest estimate (0.928) from a multimodal model lacking clinical predictors. Only two studies compared clinical-only with combined models (AUC increments of 0.060 and 0.081). Conclusions Reported discrimination was generally high, but current evidence cannot establish that radiomics adds value beyond routine clinical predictors. These models are best understood as predictive biomarkers rather than detection tools; a potential triage role among patients below routine staging thresholds remains untested, and transportability beyond the high-prevalence cohorts studied is unproven; prospective multicentre validation is required before clinical use.
originalAbstract:
Introduction

Whether bone metastasis is present at diagnosis determines curative versus systemic treatment of prostate cancer, yet referral for advanced staging relies on imperfect risk stratification; magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) radiomics has been proposed to predict metastatic status from routinely acquired staging imaging.

Methods

This systematic review (PROSPERO CRD420261463568) searched PubMed, Embase and Cochrane CENTRAL for studies of radiomic, deep-learning or hybrid models predicting bone-metastatic status from prostate MRI; incremental value over clinical predictors, reporting completeness, radiomics methodology and risk of bias were appraised.

Results

Six retrospective studies (1240 patients, 491 with bone metastasis, all from China; 322 contributed to the principal validation estimates) were included. Clinical-plus-radiomics models achieved validation areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) of 0.893-0.920 internally and 0.903 externally, with the highest estimate (0.928) from a multimodal model lacking clinical predictors. Only two studies compared clinical-only with combined models (AUC increments of 0.060 and 0.081).

Conclusions

Reported discrimination was generally high, but current evidence cannot establish that radiomics adds value beyond routine clinical predictors. These models are best understood as predictive biomarkers rather than detection tools; a potential triage role among patients below routine staging thresholds remains untested, and transportability beyond the high-prevalence cohorts studied is unproven; prospective multicentre validation is required before clinical use.

title: Brain Microstructural Alterations in Children with Tuberous Sclerosis Complex: A Neurite Orientation Dispersion and Density Imaging Study.
abstract: Objective: To evaluate brain microstructural alterations in children with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) using neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) and to investigate associations between NODDI parameters and clinical phenotypes including epilepsy, early-onset epilepsy, infantile epileptic spasms, status epilepticus, and drug-resistant epilepsy. Methods: This prospective cross-sectional study enrolled 68 children with TSC and 39 healthy controls (sex-matched; the groups differed significantly in age, which was adjusted for in all analyses, with spline modeling and pediatric-range sensitivity analyses) who underwent multi-shell diffusion MRI. NODDI parameters neurite density index (NDI), orientation dispersion index (ODI), and isotropic volume fraction (FISO) were computed. Group differences were assessed using Mann-Whitney U tests, with additional analyses adjusting for age. Logistic regression examined associations between NODDI parameters and clinical variables. Receiver operating characteristic analysis evaluated discriminative performance within the derivation cohort, with bootstrap and cross-validated internal validation. Results: The TSC group demonstrated significantly reduced whole-brain NDI, ODI, and FISO compared to controls after adjusting for age (all p ≤ 0.001). TSC patients with epilepsy showed significantly lower NDI (p < 0.001), ODI (p = 0.001), and FISO (p = 0.003) versus controls, whereas patients without epilepsy showed no significant differences. Early-onset epilepsy and infantile epileptic spasms were associated with marked NDI reductions (16.7% and 19.0%, respectively; p < 0.001). In a parsimonious model, NDI was associated with epilepsy (p = 0.008; bootstrap-corrected AUC 0.712); in an exploratory multivariable model, NDI (p = 0.008) and ODI (p = 0.035) were associated with epilepsy after adjustment. NDI achieved an AUC of 0.739 (95% CI 0.617-0.861) with 65.5% sensitivity and 78.8% specificity at a cutoff of 0.095, reflecting discrimination within the derivation cohort. Conclusions: NODDI sensitively detects widespread brain microstructural alterations in children with TSC. NDI, and to a lesser extent ODI after adjustment, show significant associations with epilepsy and may serve as quantitative imaging markers of epilepsy-associated microstructural burden; however, the cross-sectional design cannot establish whether these alterations are caused by epilepsy or reflect the underlying TSC disease process, and whether they predict future epilepsy onset or outcome requires longitudinal, externally validated studies. The significant age difference between groups, which statistical adjustment cannot fully resolve, is a key limitation. NODDI is best viewed as one component of a multimodal biomarker framework that also incorporates molecular, immune and electrophysiological measures.

title: The Lateral Mesencephalic Sulcus as a Layered Posterolateral Microsurgical Corridor: A Cadaveric Fiber Dissection and MRI Morphometric Study.
abstract: This study aimed to describe the sequential microsurgical relationships surrounding the lateral mesencephalic sulcus (LMS) through fiber dissection and characterize regional anatomical variation using MRI morphometry in an independent adult cohort. Eight formalin-fixed adult specimens underwent stepwise fiber dissection. T2-weighted MRI examinations from 100 adults were retrospectively analyzed. Measurements included the inferior colliculus-straight sinus angle (ICSSA), corpus callosum-pontomesencephalic junction distance (CCPJD), LMS-midline angle (LMS-MA), LMS-midline distance (LMS-MD), and LMS-cerebellar surface distance (LMS-CSD). The splenium-mesencephalon relationship (SMR) was categorized descriptively. Comparisons and age correlations were evaluated using Holm-adjusted p values. Dissection documented sequential relationships between the LMS, lemniscal pathways, superior cerebellar peduncle, and deep tegmental structures. The MRI cohort included 50 women and 50 men aged 23-88 years. Mean ICSSA was 29.6 ± 5.3° and CCPJD was 24.17 ± 3.85 mm. Right and left values were 21.9 ± 3.9° and 22.2 ± 4.0° for LMS-MA, 9.77 ± 0.81 and 9.91 ± 0.84 mm for LMS-MD, and 6.12 ± 1.87 and 6.28 ± 1.68 mm for LMS-CSD. No right-left differences remained significant after correction. Males had greater left LMS-MD and right LMS-CSD (adjusted p = 0.002 and 0.004, respectively). Age correlated negatively with CCPJD (ρ = -0.389; adjusted p < 0.001) and positively with right and left LMS-CSD (ρ = 0.268 and 0.379; adjusted p = 0.042 and <0.001, respectively). SMR Types A, B, and C occurred in 70%, 29%, and 1%, respectively. Fiber dissection and MRI morphometry provide complementary descriptive anatomical reference data. The MRI parameters characterize regional variation; their correspondence with deep microsurgical boundaries and clinical applicability remain to be established.

title: Selective White Matter Volume Reduction in Neurologically Asymptomatic Adults with Obesity: An AI-Based MRI Volumetric Study.
abstract: Background and Objectives: Obesity has been associated with structural brain alterations and an increased long-term risk of cognitive decline; however, the regional distribution and tissue specificity of these changes remain inconsistent across neuroimaging studies. This study investigated global and regional brain volume differences in neurologically asymptomatic and cognitively preserved adults with obesity using automated artificial intelligence-based MRI volumetric analysis. Materials and Methods: This cross-sectional study included 100 adults, comprising 50 participants with obesity (body mass index (BMI) ≥ 30 kg/m2) and 50 adults with normal-weight considered as controls (BMI 18.5-24.9 kg/m2) matched for age and sex. All participants underwent standardized brain MRI on the same 1.5 T scanner, including a high-resolution 3D T1-weighted sequence. Brain segmentation and volumetric analysis were performed using AIRS Medical SwiftSight-Brain. Primary analyses used volumes normalized to total intracranial volume (TIV). Group differences were evaluated using effect-size estimates and linear models adjusted for age and sex; exploratory region-of-interest analyses were corrected for multiple comparisons. Results: Participants with obesity had lower cerebral white matter volume than controls (29.43 ± 1.80% vs. 30.21 ± 1.21% TIV; p = 0.014; Hedges' g = -0.50), and the difference remained significant after adjustment for age and sex (β = -0.768 percentage points, 95% CI -1.368 to -0.167; p = 0.013). Regionally, temporal white matter (4.69 ± 0.31% vs. 4.86 ± 0.23% TIV; adjusted p = 0.0018), parietal white matter (7.09 ± 0.48% vs. 7.34 ± 0.36% TIV; adjusted p = 0.0045), and cerebellar white matter (1.70 ± 0.13% vs. 1.77 ± 0.13% TIV; adjusted p = 0.009) were lower in the obesity group. Whole-brain/TIV was also lower after age and sex adjustment (β = -0.907 percentage points; 95% CI -1.655 to -0.158; p = 0.018), whereas cortical gray matter volume was virtually identical between groups (p = 0.960). No significant difference in hippocampal volume was observed. Conclusions: Neurologically asymptomatic and cognitively preserved adults with obesity exhibited subtle, regionally selective brain volume differences, with the most pronounced alterations involving cerebral white matter, particularly of temporal and parietal lobes. These findings suggest that obesity-related brain vulnerability may be detectable before clinically manifest cognitive impairment and may preferentially involve white matter rather than widespread cortical gray matter loss.

title: Predicting Risk of Conversion to Clinically Diagnosed Alzheimer's Disease from Baseline sMRI Using Supervised Functional Principal Component Analysis.
abstract: Accurate prediction of the risk of progression to clinically diagnosed Alzheimer's Disease (AD) in cognitively normal (CN) individuals and those with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is essential for early intervention and prognosis. Structural magnetic resonance imaging (sMRI) provides rich information on brain morphology, but its high dimensionality poses challenges for robust risk prediction, especially with limited sample sizes and censored outcomes. In this study, we extend a prediction-oriented framework based on supervised functional principal component analysis (sFPCA) to extract low-dimensional components from baseline sMRI data in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort. sFPCA extracts components that balance dominant imaging variation against their association with the survival outcome, thereby reducing the dimensionality of the sMRI data while retaining relevant imaging information. The resulting components were evaluated using both Cox proportional hazards (Cox PHs) and random survival forest (RSF) models, providing complementary log-linear and nonparametric survival-prediction frameworks. Across ten retained development/test partitions, mean test IAUC was 0.7733 for sFPCA-Cox and 0.7294 for sFPCA-RSF, with corresponding Integrated Brier Scores (IBSs) of 0.08730 and 0.09232, respectively. The matched uFPCA models achieved mean IAUC values of 0.7719 and 0.7357 under Cox PH and RSF, respectively, indicating that the incremental predictive contribution of survival supervision was modest and depended on the downstream survival model. While the primary objective is risk prediction, additional analysis results based on low-, middle- and high-risk groups are used to facilitate interpretation of the learned imaging components. The identified anatomical spatial patterns involve regions such as the hippocampus, amygdala, and prefrontal and temporal cortices, supporting their relevance to AD-related neurodegeneration. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of sMRI-based prediction of conversion to clinically diagnosed AD and suggest that survival supervision may provide modest improvements under some modeling configurations.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Colorectal Cancer Diagnosis: A Comprehensive Survey of Modalities, Frameworks, and Clinical Tasks.
abstract: The diagnosis of colorectal cancer encompasses nine complementary modalities: stool-based screening, blood-based biomarkers, cross-sectional imaging, endoscopic evaluation, histopathology, liquid biopsy, molecular and genetic profiling, microbiome analysis, and nanotechnology-based diagnostics. This narrative review synthesizes 160 references spanning seven task-specific artificial intelligence domains, including computer-aided detection, optical diagnosis, invasion depth prediction, computational pathology and radiogenomics, metastasis forecasting, neoadjuvant treatment response prediction, and surgical workflow analysis. We propose a conceptual multimodal pipeline comprising data ingestion, preprocessing and harmonization, feature representation, multimodal fusion, forecasting, explainability, and validation. A structured evidence grading framework classifies each clinical task by evidence level, consistency, and clinical readiness. We further catalog public datasets, challenge benchmarks, and five reporting standards: TRIPOD-AI, CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT-AI, DECIDE-AI, and CLAIM. Computer-aided detection and optical diagnosis demonstrate the highest maturity with Level 1 evidence from randomized controlled trials, while computational pathology, radiogenomics, and metastasis prediction remain at Level 2 with retrospective validation (internal or external). Microbiome screening, nanotechnology diagnostics, and surgical phase recognition are exploratory. The principal barriers to clinical adoption are domain shift, data scarcity, calibration, prospective validation, and workflow integration. We conclude that clinically useful artificial intelligence requires robust external validation, uncertainty quantification, explainable outputs, standardized reporting, and a structured translational pathway from retrospective evidence through regulatory clearance to post-deployment monitoring.

title: PET/MRI in Oncology: Real-World Recommendations.
abstract: Positron emission tomography/magnetic resonance imaging (PET/MRI) has represented a paradigm shift in medical imaging, and although its use has not yet been fully incorporated into all clinical guidelines, scientific evidence supports its ability to provide a highly accurate simultaneous metabolic and anatomical assessment, which is particularly useful for staging, treatment planning, and evaluating treatment response in cancer patients. The limited availability of the technique and the demands it places on resources and coordination suggest that its initial use should focus on those applications that can provide the greatest benefit to patients, especially within the indications related to oncological processes, where PET and MRI have a defined and complementary role. This review focuses specifically on some of these conditions.

title: Explainable DSC Perfusion Radiomics for Post-Treatment Glioblastoma Assessment Using a Soft-Voting Machine-Learning Ensemble.
abstract: Background/objectives After chemoradiation for glioblastoma, residual or recurrent tumor (tumor-positive disease, TP) and treatment-related change (TRC), which includes pseudoprogression and radiation necrosis, look alike on conventional MRI. We tested whether radiomic features from dynamic susceptibility contrast (DSC) perfusion MRI alone can separate them. Methods We analyzed 224 post-treatment MRI examinations from 168 patients in the public UCSD-PTGBM collection. A machine-learning ensemble was trained on 1223 radiomic features from the leakage-corrected relative cerebral blood volume (rCBV) map, with training (109 patients, 143 examinations) and test (59 patients, 81 examinations) data separated at the patient level and the model fixed before testing. The analysis was repeated on the cerebral blood flow (CBF) map from the same scans, and DSC was compared with arterial spin labeling (ASL) in patients who had both. Results On the independent test set (patient-level analysis), the model distinguished TP from TRC with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.79 (95% CI 0.67-0.89). It detected 31 of 49 patients with tumor (sensitivity 63%) and correctly identified all 10 patients with TRC (specificity 100%); at a predefined higher-sensitivity cut-off, sensitivity was 69% and specificity 80%. With the CBF map, the AUC did not differ significantly (0.78; p = 0.89), but there was a different balance of sensitivity and specificity. In an exploratory subset of 36 patients, DSC and ASL did not differ significantly (AUC 0.82 vs. 0.71; p = 0.52). Conclusions DSC perfusion radiomics alone identified tumor with high specificity but missed about one-third of tumors: a positive result may support a diagnosis of tumor, whereas a negative result cannot exclude it. External, multicenter validation is needed before clinical use.

After chemoradiation for glioblastoma, residual or recurrent tumor (tumor-positive disease, TP) and treatment-related change (TRC), which includes pseudoprogression and radiation necrosis, look alike on conventional MRI. Methods

We analyzed 224 post-treatment MRI examinations from 168 patients in the public UCSD-PTGBM collection. A machine-learning ensemble was trained on 1223 radiomic features from the leakage-corrected relative cerebral blood volume (rCBV) map, with training (109 patients, 143 examinations) and test (59 patients, 81 examinations) data separated at the patient level and the model fixed before testing. The analysis was repeated on the cerebral blood flow (CBF) map from the same scans, and DSC was compared with arterial spin labeling (ASL) in patients who had both.

On the independent test set (patient-level analysis), the model distinguished TP from TRC with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.79 (95% CI 0.67-0.89). It detected 31 of 49 patients with tumor (sensitivity 63%) and correctly identified all 10 patients with TRC (specificity 100%); at a predefined higher-sensitivity cut-off, sensitivity was 69% and specificity 80%. With the CBF map, the AUC did not differ significantly (0.78; p = 0.89), but there was a different balance of sensitivity and specificity. In an exploratory subset of 36 patients, DSC and ASL did not differ significantly (AUC 0.82 vs. 0.71; p = 0.52).

Conclusions

DSC perfusion radiomics alone identified tumor with high specificity but missed about one-third of tumors: a positive result may support a diagnosis of tumor, whereas a negative result cannot exclude it. External, multicenter validation is needed before clinical use.

title: Vascular and Circulating Blood Exposure to Proton or Photon Irradiation: Differentials in Lymphocyte Subset Metrics in Cancer Patients.
abstract: Background/objectives Radiation-induced lymphopenia is consistently associated with adverse outcomes across solid tumours, yet the vascular compartment that carries the irradiated lymphocyte pool is not routinely delineated during treatment planning. The VASA project makes blood vessels an explicit, measurable structure in that process. Phase II aimed primarily to establish the feasibility of that delineation and secondarily to explore how dose-volume metrics computed on MRI-segmented vessels relate to serial immunophenotyping in patients treated with protons or photons. Methods Thirty-nine patients treated between March 2021 and May 2022 were studied prospectively (30 proton, 9 photon). Flow-contrast three-dimensional MRI with three velocity-encoding directions was added to simulation; vessel masks segmented semi-automatically from the sum-of-magnitude reconstruction were imported into the treatment-planning system to generate dose-volume histograms. The effective dose to circulating immune cells (EDIC), the integral dose to vessels (IDVe) and the integral dose to target were computed. Blood was sampled at the start and at the end of irradiation for lymphocyte counts and B, T and NK immunophenotyping. Groups were compared with Welch's t -test for continuous variables and Fisher's exact test for categorical variables, without correction for multiple comparisons; the photon subgroup was not matched. Results EDIC was higher with photons than protons (5.60 vs. 1.25 Gy; p = 0.005) and in patients who became lymphopenic (4.84 vs. 1.47 Gy; p = 0.027); IDVe differed in the same direction without reaching significance (3.60 vs. 0.53 Gy·L, p = 0.091; 3.08 vs. 0.67 Gy·L, p = 0.180). Within the proton cohort, EDIC and IDVe increased from brain to head-and-neck to thorax-abdomen targets (0.81, 1.11 and 2.17 Gy; 0.13, 0.26 and 1.63 Gy·L), and the IDVe ordering persisted after adjustment for target volume ( p < 0.001). Lymphocyte counts fell from 1.92 to 1.43 × 10 3 /µL in the proton cohort ( p < 0.001), with the lowest end-of-treatment values in thorax-abdomen targets (1.31 × 10 3 /µL). B, T and NK subpopulations all declined in the proton cohort; among regions, only head-and-neck targets showed significant T and NK losses. Conclusions Patient-specific vascular delineation and dosimetry are feasible in a clinical planning workflow, and the resulting metrics track irradiation modality and the magnitude of lymphocyte depletion. These associations are exploratory; immune-sparing plan optimisation using vascular constraints remains a future application requiring prospective validation.

title: Realistic Performance Estimation in Small-Cohort Deep Learning and Machine Learning: A Leakage-Controlled Codebase Applied to Meningioma Response Prediction After Gamma Knife Radiosurgery.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Deep learning may support the prediction of meningioma response after Gamma Knife radiosurgery (GKRS), but small clinical cohorts increase the risk of overfitting and unstable performance. We developed leakage-controlled code adjusted for small clinical datasets. Methods: Pretreatment contrast-enhanced T1 MRI from 190 patients was analysed using one tumour-centred axial slice per patient. Response was defined as a tumour volume decrease ≥ 30% per log 10 (months). ResNet-10t, ResNet-18, ResNet-50 and DenseNet-121 with ImageNet or RadImageNet pretraining were evaluated in three workflows: (1) frozen backbone CNN, head-only training; (2) logistic regression or naive Bayes classification of features extracted from frozen CNNs; and (3) restricted CNN fine-tuning. Five partially overlapping chronological development/test splits were assessed, with all data-dependent fitting, feature selection and model optimisation restricted to development data. Results: The smallest RadImageNet ResNet-10t CNN performed best when fine-tuned (peak AUCs 0.953 and 1.000) but showed the widest split-to-split variation (range 0.738-1.000). When RadImageNet features extracted from ResNet-10t were classified by naive Bayes and logistic regression, they reached lower median and peak AUCs but within narrower ranges. Predictive performance did not consistently depend on CNN size. Conclusions: To our knowledge, this is the first deep learning study predicting volumetric meningioma response after GKRS. We provide openly available, ready-to-use code for three major workflows in small clinical datasets, with safeguards against information leakage. The benefit of fine-tuning and of RadImageNet pretraining depended on architecture. Robust small-cohort modelling requires attention to performance consistency across chronological splits, not only to the highest AUC in a single split.

title: Perfusion MRI for Preoperative Grading of Intracranial Meningiomas: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Background/Objectives: A reliable preoperative estimate of World Health Organization (WHO) grade 2-3 meningiomas could complement existing criteria when planning surgery and follow-up. We assessed whether perfusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) parameters differ between grade 1 and grade 2-3 meningiomas. Methods: PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science were searched to 6 October 2026 (OSF registration 10.17605/OSF.IO/G3Q9M). Standardised mean differences (Hedges' g) of dynamic susceptibility contrast (DSC), dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) or arterial spin labelling (ASL) parameters were pooled with random-effects models, separately for intratumoral and peritumoral measurements. Risk of bias was assessed with the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool and certainty with the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. Results: Ten studies (509 patients; 129 with grade 2-3 tumours) were included. Intratumoral relative cerebral blood volume (rCBV) showed no clear difference between grades (seven studies; g 0.13, 95% CI -0.71 to 0.98; p = 0.71, I2 = 84%, τ2 = 0.69). Peritumoral perfusion was higher around grade 2-3 tumours in all four studies that measured it, but the exploratory pooled estimate was imprecise (g 2.32, 95% CI -0.02 to 4.66, p = 0.051, I2 = 93%, τ2 = 2.03). Diagnostic accuracy could not be pooled. Certainty of evidence was very low. Conclusions: Current evidence does not show that intratumoral rCBV distinguishes meningioma grades. Higher peritumoral perfusion in grade 2-3 tumours, which may partly reflect peritumoral oedema, is a hypothesis to be tested in prospective studies using the 2021 WHO classification and pre-specified thresholds.

title: Few-Shot Prototype Adaptation of Frozen Pathology Foundation Models for Cross-Tissue and Cross-Cancer Transfer: From Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma to Breast Cancer Lymph Node Metastases.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Deep networks trained to recognise oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) in histopathology perform well on held-out images from the same collections, but a recent study found that such a network lost most of its discriminative ability on lymph node tissue. We examined whether encoder fine-tuning or label-free adaptation changes this, and how many labelled target patches are needed to recover performance. Methods: The source domain comprised 23,290 images of oral and oropharyngeal mucosa from three public collections. The target domain was PatchCamelyon, a public dataset of sentinel lymph node patches from breast cancer patients; its metastases are breast carcinoma, so the transfer crosses both tissue type and cancer histology. We used 40,000 target patches from 216 slides, split into slide-disjoint adaptation and evaluation pools. We compared nine encoders in ten configurations, including three pathology foundation models (Phikon, Phikon-v2 and the recent Midnight model). We evaluated direct transfer with frozen and fine-tuned encoders, label-free adaptation, and few-shot adaptation, in which we compute class prototypes from k labelled target patches using a frozen encoder. All results are at patch level. Results: Direct transfer failed for every configuration (external AUROC 0.35-0.64), including fine-tuned networks (mean over three seeds 0.44-0.52) and fine-tuned Phikon (0.54-0.58). Label-free methods did not close the gap; a zero-shot vision-language model reached 0.77. With a frozen Phikon encoder, prototypes from 10 and 50 labelled patches per class reached 0.869 ± 0.056 and 0.930 ± 0.015, against 0.82-0.86 at 50 patches for encoders without histology pre-training and 0.977 for a classifier trained on 20,000 labelled patches. Logistic regression on the same patches performed similarly at one and two patches per class and better from five upward (0.955 at 50). Midnight reached 0.922 with prototypes at 50 patches per class, similar to Phikon. The results were similar when support and evaluation patches came from different scanning centres. Conclusions: For the methods and datasets evaluated, no classifier trained on oral tissue transferred to this cross-tissue, cross-cancer target. Our analyses suggest that the change in what the classes contain mattered more than stain or scale, but they do not separate the causal contributions of tissue, cancer histology and acquisition. Frozen pathology foundation models made label-efficient classification on the target domain inexpensive; this replaces the oral-trained classifier and does not use oral images. The findings concern patch-level classification of breast cancer metastases and do not establish clinical performance for OSCC lymph node metastases.

title: Three-Dimensional Imaging, Printing, and Augmented Reality in Surgical Oncology: A Descriptive Implementation Framework at a Comprehensive Cancer Center.
abstract: Background: Three-dimensional (3D) visualization of radiological imaging has emerged as a valuable tool in surgical oncology, with applications spanning diagnostics, perioperative planning, intraoperative guidance, and patient communication. Despite its growing clinical relevance, integration into routine surgical workflows remains inconsistent and poorly standardized across specialties. Methods: We describe select cases illustrating a multispecialty feasibility and implementation experience evaluating the integration of 3D reconstruction, 3D printing, and augmented reality into surgical oncology workflows across a comprehensive cancer center. Describing cases and series of interest, we demonstrate how a structured implementation workflow was applied covering image acquisition, segmentation, volumetric rendering, and modality selection based on the specific clinical problem. A feasibility framework is proposed in terms of workflow integration, modality-to-problem fit, and clinical utility as described by the operating team. Results: Seven select case groups spanning pediatric, head and neck, urologic, gynecologic, and thoracic surgical oncology were included, with group sizes ranging from 1 to 14 patients. In 3 patients with hepatoblastoma, 3D printed anatomical models were successfully integrated into patient and family education consultations to convey tumor extent and the scope of planned resection. Segmentation-based visualization was implemented for preoperative planning in 2 patients with skull base malignancies, with the 3D workflow described as useful for operative planning by the operating team in both cases. Augmented reality (AR)-assisted 3D reconstruction was incorporated into the planning workflow for 3 patients undergoing robotic partial nephrectomy for complex renal tumors, facilitating review of vascular anatomy and assessment of the feasibility of nephron-sparing surgery. In 2 patients with suspected advanced ovarian cancer, volumetric rendering with AR was integrated into preoperative resectability planning. Among 14 patients undergoing chest wall tumor resection, patient-specific 3D printed ribcage replicas were used for preoperative implant preparation. In a separate cohort of 2 chest wall patients, AR visualization was used for spatial surgical planning. Conclusions: Across diverse oncologic contexts and surgical specialties, 3D reconstruction, printing, and augmented reality were successfully integrated into existing perioperative workflows, with each modality selected based on the specific clinical problem at hand. This experience describes a structured, modality-matched implementation framework that may serve as a practical starting point for institutions seeking to incorporate these technologies. Prospective, controlled studies are needed to establish independent clinical benefit. Broader adoption will require standardized selection criteria, prospective evaluation, and workflow adaptation for centers beyond high-volume academic institutions.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Colorectal Cancer Histopathology: From Image Analysis to Clinical Translation-A Systematic Review.
abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are increasingly applied to haematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained colorectal cancer (CRC) histopathology, but it remains unclear how far reported performance reflects readiness for clinical use. Following PRISMA 2020, PubMed and Scopus were searched to 30 August 2026, and two reviewers independently selected studies; 102 studies were included. Each was classified by principal task, level of analysis, and validation strategy, and risk of bias was assessed with an adapted QUADAS-2 tool. Most studies addressed binary tumour-versus-benign classification (53.9%) or multiclass tissue classification (26.5%); dysplasia grading, segmentation, and molecular prediction were less common. Over half evaluated isolated patches, 62.7% relied on public datasets, and only 21.6% tested a fixed model on an independent external cohort. Only 6 (5.9%) studies were at low risk of bias. Near-perfect accuracies came mainly from randomly partitioned benchmarks, performance declined on independent cohorts, and no study reported a prospective trial. This systematic review provides a task- and validation-stratified appraisal of CNNs in CRC histopathology, showing that the main barrier to clinical adoption is no longer algorithmic accuracy but the quality of validation evidence. Patient-level data separation, multicentre external validation, slide-level evaluation, and prospective evaluation of pathologist-AI collaboration are priorities.

title: Tumor-Secreted microRNAs as Circulating Biomarkers for Lung Cancer Detection and Prognostic Stratification.
abstract: Background: Early lung cancer detection remains challenging. Low-dose CT screening reduces mortality but is limited by false positives and low uptake. Circulating miRNAs are stable blood biomarkers, but reproducibility is poor as most derive from non-tumor tissues. We hypothesized that miRNAs secreted by lung cancer cells would provide more grounded biomarkers. Methods: Small RNA sequencing was performed on paired intracellular and extracellular RNA from conditioned media of six NSCLC cell lines and non-malignant controls. Differentially expressed miRNAs enriched in cancer-derived fractions were identified. Candidates were validated in serum from NSCLC patients and controls by RT-qPCR and examined in TCGA cohorts. Pathway and survival analyses assessed relevance. Results: Extracellular miRNA profiles were conserved across NSCLC lines and distinct from intracellular profiles. A core set of 25 miRNAs was enriched in cancer-derived media. Five miRNAs (miR-10b, miR-25, miR-92a, miR-182, miR-375) were elevated in NSCLC serum and robustly expressed in TCGA tumors. Pathway analysis showed enrichment of PI3K-Akt and hypoxia signaling. Elevated miR-10b was associated with poorer survival. Conclusions: Lung cancer cells secrete a conserved miRNA set detectable in serum and tumors, linked to oncogenic pathways and survival. Cell-based profiling offers a strategy for developing plasma miRNA assays for lung cancer detection.

title: Serial Circulating Tumour Cell Monitoring During Androgen Deprivation and Docetaxel Therapies Identifies Poor Prognostic Metastatic Prostate Cancer.
abstract: Adding docetaxel to androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) prolongs survival in metastatic prostate cancer, but not all patients benefit, and no early biomarker identifies individuals with resistant disease. We assessed whether serial circulating tumour cell (CTC) sampling adds prognostic information beyond a pre-treatment sample. CTCs were enriched by size and deformability (Parsortix®) and phenotyped as epithelial (CK+/VIM-/CD45-), mesenchymal (CK-/VIM+/CD45-), or EMTing (CK+/VIM+/CD45-) at four time points in 61 patients treated with ADT and docetaxel (43 hormone-sensitive; 18 resistant, exploratory). With longer follow-up, our previously reported baseline CTC predictors remained associated with overall survival (OS). In hormone-sensitive patients, baseline ≥ 6 total (HR 3.21, p = 0.007) and epithelial CTCs (p = 0.017) were associated with shorter OS. Across baseline, early, and late treatment, the OS hazard ratio for epithelial CTCs fell (2.59, 2.29, 2.11), yet for ≥3 mesenchymal CTCs rose (1.99, 2.99, 4.08). No single time point result survived false-discovery-rate correction. During early treatment, radiographic responders had fewer mesenchymal CTCs than non-responders (median 0 vs. 2.5, p = 0.032), whereas PSA did not differ (p = 0.642). Persistence of ≥3 mesenchymal CTCs from baseline to late treatment identified the poorest outcome (n = 3; median OS 17.3 months vs. not reached) and survived false-discovery-rate correction (q = 0.019). Late treatment mesenchymal CTCs added value to baseline PSA (p = 0.024) and ALP (p = 0.019) and added potential value to the best baseline marker (≥6 CTCs, p = 0.125), identifying some high-risk patients with baseline < 6 CTCs. Early on-treatment CTC samples may help predict response, while late treatment mesenchymal CTCs may add to baseline clinical markers. These hypothesis-generating findings require validation in a larger prospective cohort.

title: Attention-Based Dual-Branch Deep Learning for Overall Survival Prediction in Patients with Brain Metastases Using MRI: A Multicenter Retrospective Study.
abstract: Objectives: To develop and validate an attention-based deep learning (DL) model to predict overall survival (OS) in patients with brain metastases (BM) using pre-treatment magnetic resonance image (MRI). Methods: A total of 216 BM patients treated with radiotherapy or neurosurgical resection were retrospectively enrolled from two hospitals and divided into training (n = 128), internal validation (n = 56), and external validation (n = 32) cohorts. Three feature aggregation methods and seven radiomics models were developed to predict OS. A DL model named DeepBMSurv, incorporating a cross-attention mechanism, was built using pre-treatment MR images. Its prognostic performance was compared with radiomics models and graded prognostic assessment (GPA). A nomogram integrating GPA, radiomics score (Rad-score) and DL score (DL_RiskScore) was also developed. Model performance was assessed by the concordance index (C-index). Results: Among the radiomics models, the RadScoremean model showed the most stable discrimination across cohorts, with C-index values of 0.685, 0.672, and 0.671 in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts. DeepBMSurv achieved numerically higher C-indices than both the radiomics model and GPA model, with C-indices of 0.806 vs. 0.685 vs. 0.620 in the training cohort, 0.755 vs. 0.672 vs. 0.628 in the internal validation cohort, and 0.733 vs. 0.671 vs. 0.579 in the external validation cohort. The nomogram integrating DL_RiskScore, Rad-score, and GPA achieved C-index values of 0.809, 0.764 and 0.733 in training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, respectively. Conclusions: A DL model based on pre-treatment MRI can effectively predict survival outcomes in patients with BM, offering a potential tool for individualized prognostic risk stratification.

title: Advances in Radiotherapy for Glioblastoma and IDH-Mutant High-Grade Astrocytoma: A Biological and Mechanistic Perspective.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) and IDH-mutant high-grade astrocytoma remain therapeutically challenging. Historical GBM chemoradiation trials reported median overall survival of approximately 15-17 months; contemporary outcomes vary with molecular features, patient selection, and additional therapies. The 60 Gy in 30 fractions partial-brain regimen remains the reference standard for fit patients with newly diagnosed GBM. This narrative review examines radiotherapy based on its underlying biology, distinguishing GBM from IDH-mutant astrocytoma under the WHO molecular framework. It links DNA damage, cell-death programs, and radiation-induced immune signaling to the treatment response and DNA repair, stemness, hypoxia, and the microenvironment to resistance. These mechanisms motivate DNA-damage-response inhibitors, molecularly matched radiosensitizers, and immunotherapy combinations. Tumor treating fields are considered as an adjunctive non-ionizing modality. Proton therapy, FLASH, and MRI-guided adaptive radiotherapy are evaluated for their rationale and normal-tissue effects. Neurocognitive injury is discussed alongside the limitations of proposed hippocampal-sparing objectives. Personalization requires molecular selection and mechanism-matched treatment, with the clinical validation of benefits beyond dosimetry or imaging alone.

title: Does Learning from Unlabeled Data Help Cancer Diagnosis and Prognosis? Semi-Supervised and Self-Supervised Learning Versus Tabular Foundation Model.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Machine learning for cancer diagnosis and prognosis requires costly patient labels. Semi- and self-supervised methods exploit unlabeled data but are rarely tested against equivalent supervised models. We tested whether unlabeled data help and compared these methods with a tabular foundation model. Methods: Four public breast cancer datasets (WDBC, Mammography, METABRIC, SEER) crossed clinical task (diagnosis, including the detection of microcalcifications on Mammography, or prognosis) with class balance. In five-fold cross-validation with five seeds, 10%, 20%, or 50% of training records were labeled. Self-training (random forest and XGBoost), label spreading, and SCARF self-supervised pretraining were each compared with a matched supervised control; logistic regression and TabPFN v2 were references. Analyses used corrected resampled t-tests with Holm adjustment, Bayesian correlated and hierarchical tests, and power analysis. Results: Of 96 comparisons with matched controls in the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) and the area under the precision-recall curve (PR-AUC), three were significant, all involving SCARF: two losses on Mammography and one PR-AUC gain on METABRIC that persisted with all labels. The estimated minimum detectable effects at 80% power varied across comparisons, with medians of approximately 0.06 in PR-AUC and 0.09 in MCC; the median absolute observed differences were 0.008 and 0.015, respectively. At the default threshold and 10% labels, label spreading lowered sensitivity on SEER (-0.135) and random-forest self-training on Mammography (-0.122). TabPFN had the highest PR-AUC in all 16 settings. Conclusions: Under the evaluated datasets, methods and settings, no statistically significant additional benefit from unlabeled data beyond shared preprocessing was detected, but the evidence does not establish equivalence; TabPFN achieved the highest PR-AUC in every setting. New methods should be tested against matched controls and tabular foundation models with adequate power.

title: Selective Late-Timepoint 68 Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT in Prostate Cancer: A Management-Focused Framework.
abstract: 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT has the most established evidence base among PSMA-targeted imaging agents for prostate cancer and is incorporated into clinical guidelines internationally for initial staging, prostate-specific antigen (PSA) persistence, biochemical recurrence (BCR), and selection for PSMA-directed therapy. Its integration into routine clinical practice reflects established acquisition workflows and consistently high diagnostic performance, including localization of small-volume nodal and distant disease that may be occult on conventional imaging. Imaging is generally performed approximately 60 min after 68Ga-PSMA-11 administration; however, interest in additional image acquisition at a later timepoint (i.e., late-timepoint imaging) has emerged, with evidence from published studies and real-world experience from centers of excellence supporting feasibility and utility for select clinical scenarios. This additional late (generally 90 min to 3 h) acquisition may improve lesion-to-background contrast or help characterize low-level uptake, indeterminate findings, and suspected recurrence adjacent to physiologic urinary activity. However, improved contrast or lesion detection does not consistently translate into changes in clinical management, supporting selective rather than routine use. In this narrative review, we synthesize published evidence and expert clinical experience to define the potential role of late-timepoint 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT. We position late-timepoint imaging as a selective, management-focused strategy that can provide complementary information when the standard acquisition leaves a clinically actionable question unresolved. The highest-value applications include early BCR with uncertain local-only versus local-plus-regional nodal recurrence, indeterminate pelvic or metastatic uptake, and suspected local recurrence adjacent to physiologic urinary activity. In appropriately selected cases, a late acquisition may be readily integrated into the established PET workflow using the same imaging system and acquisition framework, enabling patient-specific temporal or postvoid information to refine staging and support individualized treatment planning. We propose a management-anchored framework and practical workflow, based on published literature and clinical experience, to support selective, operationally feasible, and patient-centered use.

title: Single-Fraction Stereotactic Radiosurgery for Spontaneous Canine Brain Tumours Under Human Hospital Standards: A Feasibility Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Standard radiotherapy (RT) protocols for spontaneous canine brain tumours, consisting of multiple fractions delivered over several weeks, impose a considerable burden on patients and owners. Single-fraction stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) represents an attractive alternative, but no study has previously reported this approach for canine glioma treatment conducted under human patient clinical and regulatory standards. Methods: Five pet dogs with presumptive glioma diagnosis based on MRI criteria were treated with a single fraction of linac-generated X-rays delivering 10 Gy to the planning target volume, using three to five non-coplanar arcs of a 6 MV beam at the Grenoble Alps University Hospital. Follow-up consisted of clinical exams, MRI and owner-estimated quality of life (QoL) assessment. Five further dogs were treated with a single 15 Gy RT fraction. Three non-irradiated dogs receiving medical management only served as controls. Results: During the first three months after 10 Gy exposure, QoL improved from 7.1 to 8.3 out of 10. Tumour volume reduced by 57% at one month and by 75% at three months post RT, with a reduction observed in all five dogs. Progressive disease was noted at six and nine months after treatment. Two dogs had no evidence of tumour progression at the time of death due to abdominal diseases. Median survival time of dogs receiving 10 or 15 Gy or without irradiation reached 281, 325, and 27 days, respectively (p < 0.005). A 15 Gy RT fraction led to imaging findings suggestive of radiation-induced injury in four of five dogs at the time of death. Conclusions: Single-fraction hospital SRS is technically feasible, safe, and effective for spontaneous canine glioma when conducted under human clinical and regulatory standards. A single 10 Gy fraction was well tolerated and associated with tumour response, whereas 15 Gy appeared to approach the tolerance limit of the normal brain. Preliminary clinical outcomes are encouraging, but further validation in larger cohorts is required. This canine model provides a reproducible linac-based reference arm for the optimisation and comparative validation of innovative RT modalities, bridging the gap between preclinical rodent studies and human clinical translation.

title: Bone Marrow Biopsy in the PET/CT Era: Its Role in Hodgkin and Common B-Cell Lymphomas: A Contemporary Narrative Review.
abstract: Background: Bone marrow biopsy (BMB) provides histological information that complements whole-body fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (FDG PET/CT). Its clinical value varies across lymphoma subtypes and extends beyond staging. Methods: This narrative review synthesizes the literature identified through PubMed, Scopus and ScienceDirect searches, supplemented by purposively selected guidelines, foundational studies and citation-linked publications. Recent evidence was prioritized, with older studies retained where needed to explain changes in practice. The synthesis distinguishes diagnostic accuracy, stage migration and consequences for patient management. Results: Routine staging BMB can generally be omitted in PET-staged Hodgkin lymphoma and in DLBCL without a management-changing question about discordant or alternative marrow pathology. Marrow assessment remains part of guideline-based evaluation in FL, MCL and nodal or splenic MZL, particularly when localized treatment, unexplained cytopenias or diagnostic classification makes the result consequential. Pooled PET/CT sensitivity for FL marrow involvement was 67% (95% confidence interval, 38-87%). In one MCL cohort, the PET/CT-negative predictive value was 27.8% at a composite marrow involvement prevalence of 78.4%, illustrating the importance of disease prevalence and reference standards. FDG avidity of extra-nodal MZL lesions does not establish reliable detection of marrow infiltration. Aspirate-based ancillary tests can clarify clonal or alternative pathology, while ctDNA, radiomics and PET/MRI remain complementary approaches. Conclusions: Marrow sampling should answer a defined clinical question. Subtype-specific guidance, laboratory abnormalities and the likely consequences of additional tissue information provide the basis for deciding when biopsy is useful.
